summary: This RFC reproduces the National Research Council report that compared the DoD Internet Protocol and TCP with the ISO Internet Protocol and Transport Protocol class 4 (TP-4).

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 942 reproduces a 1985 study for the Department of Defense and the National Bureau of Standards about a choice of transport protocol. The Defense Department used TCP; the standards bureau used the ISO standard called TP-4; and the two could not talk to each other. The committee weighed the technical differences, the cost of changing, and the value of using commercial products, and recommended a careful move to the ISO protocols.

subtitle: A government study comparing the DoD's TCP with the ISO transport protocol, and what it recommended.

tldr.problem: The Department of Defense and the National Bureau of Standards had each promulgated a transport protocol as a standard, and the two were incompatible. The DoD had a large investment in TCP-based networks and an operational need to interoperate with allies and other agencies that were moving to ISO standards.
tldr.mechanism: A National Research Council committee compared the two protocol sets function by function at the transport and internet layers, measured the market and cost arguments, and set out three options with their risks, costs and benefits. It found TCP and TP-4 functionally equivalent, with differences in the data interface, flow control, connection establishment and urgent data that neither protocol handled better.
tldr.outcome: The committee unanimously recommended that the DoD adopt TP-4 as a costandard with TCP and move toward exclusive use of it, while managing the transition to keep operational capability. A majority favoured adopting it immediately and a minority wanted a demonstration first; the committee was not agreed on the timetable.

today: RFC 942 is distributed for information only and does not establish any policy, and its status note says so. It reproduces a National Research Council report from February 1985 on the choice between the Department of Defense's TCP and the ISO transport protocol. It is a historical document: it has not been obsoleted or updated, and the RFC Editor's index gives it no status category.

sections.title: Why the Committee Was Formed
sections.content:
The RFC reproduces the National Research Council report resulting from a study of the DOD Internet Protocol and Transmission Control Protocol in comparison with the ISO Internet Protocol and Transport Protocol level 4. It is distributed for information only and does not establish any policy for the DARPA research community or the DDN operational community.

This is the final report of the National Research Council Committee on Computer-Computer Communication Protocols. The committee was established in May 1983 at the request of the Department of Defense and the National Bureau of Standards, Department of Commerce, to develop recommendations and guidelines for resolving differences between the two agencies on a data communications transport protocol standard.

The report notes the context: computer-based information and transaction-processing systems are basic tools in modern industry and government, and there has been a growing demand to transfer and exchange digitized data quickly and accurately, both within an organization and between organizations. Rapid electronic transport of that data requires electronic communication links, and those links are established and maintained by a layered series of procedures. Successful movement of data depends on the participants using identical or compatible procedures, or protocols. The DOD and NBS had each developed and promulgated a transport protocol as a standard, and the two protocols were dissimilar and incompatible, so the committee was called to resolve the differences.

The committee held its first meeting in August 1983 at the National Research Council in Washington, and afterwards five more two-day meetings, a three-day meeting and a one-week workshop. It was briefed by personnel from both agencies and heard from Jon Postel of the University of Southern California's Information Sciences Institute, Dave Oran of Digital Equipment Corporation, Vinton Cerf of MCI, David Wood of The Mitre Corporation, Clair Miller of Honeywell, and Robert Follett of IBM representing the Computer and Business Equipment Manufacturer's Association, and John Newman of Ultimate Corporation. The work was supported under Contract No. DCA-83-C-0051 between the US Defense Communications Agency and the National Academy of Sciences, underwritten jointly by the Department of Defense and the National Bureau of Standards.
sections.plainLanguage: Two government agencies had each written down a transport protocol and told their own suppliers to use it. The two were written differently enough that a machine using one could not talk to a machine using the other. The National Research Council put together a committee of people from industry and academia to weigh the options and recommend what the Defense Department should do.

sections.title: The Operational Needs That Drove the Choice
sections.content:
The report sets out the DOD's unique needs, which could be affected by the transport and internet protocol layers. Although all data networks must have some of these capabilities, the needs for operational readiness, mobilization and war-fighting are extreme. Survivability means some networks must function, albeit at reduced performance, after many nodes and links have been destroyed. Security means traffic patterns and data must be selectively protected through encryption, access control, auditing and routing. Precedence means systems should adjust the quality of service on the basis of priority of use, including a capability to preempt services in cases of very high priority. Robustness means the system must not fail or suffer much loss of capability because of unpredicted situations, unexpected loads or misuse; an international crisis is the strongest test of robustness, since the system must operate immediately and with virtually full performance when a situation flares up unexpectedly. Availability means the elements needed for operational readiness or fighting must be continuously available. Interoperability means different elements of the Department must be able to talk to one another, often in unpredicted ways between parties that had not planned to interoperate.

These operational needs reflect themselves into five technical or managerial needs: functional and operational specifications, in other words whether the protocol designs meet the operational needs; maximum interoperability; minimum procurement, development and support costs; ease of transition to new protocols; and manageability and responsiveness to changing DOD requirements. These are the criteria against which the DOD options for using the ISO transport and internet protocols were evaluated.

Interoperability is a very important need. Ideally, DOD networks would permit operators at any terminal to access or be accessed by applications in any computer. The Office of the Secretary of Defense has mandated the use of TCP for the Defense Communication System's Defense Data Network, unless waivers are granted, and the Defense Communication Agency is establishing standards for three higher-level utility protocols for file transfer, terminal access and electronic mail. Partly as a result of these actions, there is growing momentum toward accepting interoperability.

The report is careful about how far interoperability goes. Functional interoperability is only achieved with full generality when two communication nodes can interoperate at all protocol levels. For the DOD the relevant levels are internet, using IP; transport, using TCP; utility, using file, terminal or mail protocols; and the specific applications that use them. So if a network is developed using one transport protocol, it would generally not be able to interoperate functionally with other networks using the same transport protocol unless both networks were also using the higher-level utility and application protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The decision was not only about the protocol's features but about what the Defense Department needed from it. The report lists six: the network must survive damage, must be able to protect selected traffic, must be able to give priority to important traffic, must not fall over under surprise load, must have its parts always available, and must be able to talk to other people's systems. Interoperability was the hardest of these, because two machines can only talk fully if they agree at every level, not just the transport layer.

sections.title: How the Two Protocol Sets Differ
sections.content:
The report presents the major functional differences between the ISO and DOD protocol sets at the transport and network layers, describing them in terms of items visible to users, and then discusses particular aspects of the protocols: performance, security and risk. In summary, the services provided by TCP and TP-4 are functionally quite similar, but several functions, including the data transfer interface, flow control, connection establishment binding and out-of-band signals, are provided in significantly different ways. Neither seems intrinsically superior, but some effort would be required to convert a higher-level protocol using TCP to make use of TP-4. The report estimates that a programmer experienced with the higher-level protocols would require about six months to design, implement and test modifications of the three major DOD higher-level protocols, file transfer, mail and Telnet, to work with TP-4.

On the data transfer interface, TCP is stream oriented and delivers no End of Transmission, but accepts a push on the send side which has an effect much like an End of Transmission. TP-4 is block oriented and does deliver End of Transmission indications. On flow control, TCP has octet units of allocation, and the segment size is invisible to the user, while TP-4 has segment units of allocation, with a common segment size for both directions negotiated as part of connection establishment, which in some implementations is visible to users. On error detection, TCP applies ones-complement addition checksum while TP-4 uses an ISO algorithm, thought to be somewhat stronger, though the TCP checksum includes certain IP-level fields such as addresses, giving double protection against misdelivery. The practical difference in error-detection power is probably not important.

On simultaneous calls between the same users, TCP establishes one call while TP-4 establishes two if both sides support multiple calls, and none if they allow only one, in which case they see each other as busy. On multiple calls between the same addresses, TCP allows only one call between a given pair of source and destination ports, while TP-4 allows more than one by using reference numbers. On addressing, TCP provides 16-bit ports for addressing within a node identified by the internet layer, some assigned to well-known applications and others free for dynamic assignment, while TP-4 provides a variable-length transport suffix in the call-request packet.

On binding user entities to connections, TCP requires a prior Listen Request from a user entity before it can accept an incoming connection request, and does not queue an incoming request with no matching Listen Request but rejects the connection instead. TP-4 requires no prior request but passes a Call Indication whenever a Call Request is received, leaving open as an implementation decision how it finds or creates an appropriate user entity. The implementation guidelines indicate that well-known addresses, prior process existence and Call Request queuing may or may not be provided at the implementor's choice, which would allow different choices and hence a failure to establish a connection between standard implementations.

On out-of-band signals, TCP allows the user to specify an urgent condition at any point in the normal data stream, with several such indications combined and only the last shown to the destination, and TCP urgent messages request expedited service from the network layer. TP-4 allows users to send expedited data units carrying up to sixteen octets of user data, only half synchronised with the normal data stream, and only one can be outstanding at a time.

The committee determined that the two are sufficiently equivalent in their security-related properties that no significant technical points favor one over the other. The DOD protocol architecture assigns the security-marking function to the IP layer and provides an 11-byte security option with a defined coding in the IP header, while TP-4 provides a variable-length security option carried in Call Request packets. On precedence, TCP supports it with three bits in IP headers while TP-4 provides a 2-byte priority option in Call Request packets, and no implementations made use of precedence information at the time.

On closing, TCP provides a graceful closing mechanism that ensures all data submitted by users are delivered before the connection is terminated. The NBS TP-4 provides a similar mechanism, but it is not included in the ISO standard TP-4, which provides only an immediate disconnect service, and the report says the impact is significant if the ISO version is used, because users would have to add their own graceful termination handshake.

The internet protocols are much more similar than the transport protocols, since the DOD's IP was the basis for the ISO's IP, although reformatting, renaming and recoding of fields means the two are incompatible. The DOD IP has fixed-length 32-bit source and destination addresses plus an 8-bit protocol number field, while the ISO IP has variable-length source and destination addresses whose format is not yet specified. The DOD provides error and status reporting through the separate ICMP, including routing redirect messages, while in ISO error reporting is provided within the IP by a separate packet type. The report concludes that from the functional point of view DOD and ISO IP can be considered essentially equivalent, provided the ISO addressing scheme is suitably resolved, and that the absence of routing and control procedures from the ISO internet layer means additional procedures beyond IP would be needed to produce a complete, functioning internet even if the ISO IP were adopted.
sections.plainLanguage: The two protocols do the same job in slightly different ways, and the report walks through the differences one at a time. TCP gives the application a stream of bytes that the application must frame itself; TP-4 hands over blocks and says when a block ends. TCP counts flow control in bytes; TP-4 counts it in segments of a size agreed when the connection opens. TCP wants an application to register before calls may arrive; TP-4 passes calls to whoever is there. TCP's urgent signal rides inside the stream; TP-4 has a separate expedited channel that carries at most sixteen bytes and only one at a time. None of these is better, and the internet layers underneath are nearly the same protocol with different field encodings.

sections.title: Markets, Standards and Commercial Products
sections.content:
The report turns to the market. The DOD and NBS have each been active in protocol standardization: DARPA's research led to modern packet-switched network design, the ARPANET implemented in the early 1970s provided a testing ground for research on communications protocols, and in 1978, after four years of development, the DOD promulgated versions of TCP and an Internet Protocol and mandated their use as standards within the DOD. The report notes that TCP is now widely used and accepted, that these protocols meet the unique operational and functional requirements of the DOD, and that any changes to them are viewed with some trepidation. The Office of the Secretary of Defense has stated that standardizing TCP greatly increased the momentum within the DOD toward establishing interoperability between networks within the DOD.

The ISO side had, in the meantime, developed a new international standard Transport Protocol class 4 and a new Internetwork Protocol with the NBS Institute for Computer Sciences and Technology, in cooperation with the DOD, many industrial firms and the ISO. The ISO Transport Protocol and ISO Internetwork Protocol became Draft International Standards in September 1983 and April 1984 respectively, and commercial vendors normally consider Draft International Standards ready for implementation. Although in part derived from TCP, the new protocols are not compatible with TCP. The US standards organizations support TP-4 in international operations, and the Department of Commerce was proposing TP-4 as a Federal Information Processing Standard for use by all federal agencies.

On maturity, experimental TCP implementations were completed in 1974 at Stanford University and BBN Communications Corporation, a large number of implementations were produced between 1974 and 1982, the ARPANET switched to complete use of TCP in January 1983, and operations have been satisfactory. TP-4 had not yet been implemented in any large operational system, but it had been tested experimentally, endorsed by many commercial vendors worldwide, and substantial portions had been demonstrated at the National Computer Conference in July 1984. The report notes that the rapidity of progress in ISO surprised even its supporters, for two reasons: strong market demands from the growing integration of communications and data processing, and the progress in networking technology from ARPA and commercial developments.

The report also weighs the economic side. The DOD had a large and growing commitment in operational TCP networks, which was expected to increase by 50 to 100 percent in the next eighteen months, and this rate of investment would probably continue for the next five years for new systems and the upgrading of current ones. The report lists the networks involved, MILNET and MINET expanding and shortly to be combined, SACDIN and DODIIS undergoing major upgrading, and plans to upgrade the WWMCCS Intercomputer Network and to add separate SECRET and TOP SECRET networks, with plans to combine these six networks in the late 1980s so that they become interoperable and multilevel secure.

The report sets out the major advantages of using commercial vendor products where they meet the department's needs. Costs to the DOD for development, production and maintenance are significantly lower, because vendors spread the cost over a much larger user base, commercial vendors are generally more efficient in their operations, and vendors look for ways to improve their product to meet competition. The department generally gets more effective products, because vendors integrate the protocol functions into their entire product line. And by depending on industry to manage development and maintenance, the department can use its scarce management and technical resources on activities unique to its mission. Because the costs are so intertwined with other factors, the report says a precise estimate is impossible, and that the marginal savings should range from 30 to 80 percent.

The final argument is about direction. The DOD networks had been a model on which the ISO transport standards were built, but the rest of the world was adopting TP-4. Because the DOD represents a small fraction of the market, and because the United States supports the ISO standard, the report concludes that it is not realistic to hope that TP-4 can be altered to conform with TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: Beyond the technical comparison, the report argues from the market. TCP had fifteen years of implementations behind it and the Defense Department was investing heavily in more, but the rest of the world was buying the ISO protocols, and the ISO standards had been built on the work of the Defense Department's own networks. Since the department was a small part of the market, the report says it was not realistic to expect the ISO protocol to be bent to match TCP. Using products that industry had already built also meant lower costs and better software, with the report estimating savings of 30 to 80 percent.

sections.title: Options and the Recommendation
sections.content:
The report describes three options for the DOD. Under Option 1, the DOD would immediately modify its transport policy statement to specify TP-4 as a costandard along with TCP, develop a military specification for TP-4 covering DOD requirements for discretionary options, specify TP-4 as the preferred protocol in requests for proposals for new networks or major upgrades, and award contracts for TP-4 systems only to contractors providing commercial products, except for unique cases. Existing networks firmly committed to TCP could continue to acquire TCP implementations, with each case reviewed. United States government test facilities would be developed to validate TP-4 products, using the existing NBS validation tools as a base. Because networks based on both protocols would coexist for some time, capabilities that facilitate interoperability among networks would need to be developed, examples being gateways among networks and specialised hosts providing services such as electronic mail.

Under Option 2 the DOD would immediately announce its intention to adopt TP-4 as a transport protocol costandard with TCP after a satisfactory demonstration of its suitability for use in military networks, deferring the final commitment until the demonstration had been evaluated and TP-4 was commercially available. The demonstration should take at most eighteen months and involve development of TP-4 implementations and their installation. The difference from Option 1 is the postponement of the standard and of requests for proposals based on TP-4 until the demonstration succeeds, although provisions of Option 1 that can be completed in parallel should proceed.

Under the third option the DOD would continue using TCP as the accepted transport standard and defer any decision on TP-4 indefinitely, staying well informed on its development and working with the National Bureau of Standards on ways to transfer data between the two protocol systems.

The committee believes all three options equally satisfy the functional objectives of the DOD, including security, and that no significant differences in performance are to be expected between the protocols if the implementation is of equal quality and optimised for the environment. Option 1 gives the most rapid path to commercial products and to interoperability with external systems, with smaller development, procurement and support costs, more timely updates and wider product availability, and a shorter period of mixed operation, but involves greater risk because it commits without as complete a demonstration. Option 2 reduces the risk, because testing and demonstration precede commitment, and unit procurement costs would probably be lower because the commercial market for TP-4 will have expanded, but transition and support costs would be higher because more systems would already have been implemented with TCP, and interoperability with external networks would be delayed. Option 3 eliminates transition cost and the risk of faulty behaviour and delay, and allows the most rapid achievement of full internal interoperability with only one set of protocols, but procurement costs for TCP systems would remain high, availability of implementations would remain limited, and external interoperability would be limited and inefficient.

The basic recommendation is that the committee unanimously recommends that the DOD adopt the ISO TP-4 and IP as DOD costandards with its TCP and IP and move toward eventual exclusive use of TP-4. Transition to the ISO standards must be managed to maintain operational capabilities and minimise risks, and the timing of the transition is a major concern on which the committee was divided. A majority favoured immediate adoption of the ISO protocols as costandards with TCP, giving major procurements in 1984 and 1985 the option of using them, which is Option 1. A minority favoured deferring adoption until after a demonstration of commercial quality implementations supporting military applications, which is Option 2.

The detailed recommendations follow from that. The DOD should rapidly identify the open areas of the ISO TP-4 specifications where options for implementation are allowed and define a required subset for use in DOD systems, working with the NBS towards a federal standard with relatively few options. It should develop and implement a plan for integration of TP-4 as a costandard with TCP and for migration towards its eventual exclusive use, including dual protocol operation for some gateways, relay hosts, service hosts and terminal concentrators. It should develop a protocol test facility, using the NBS protocol-testing facility as a basis, for validation or demonstration depending on the option chosen. Procurements of new networks and major upgrades should favour ISO TP-4 as rapidly as possible. A transport service interface for TCP more like that of TP-4 should be developed and tested with existing higher-layer protocols. The DOD should continue using its own higher-level protocols for operational purposes but minimise further development of them, and the NBS should maintain close liaison with the DOD so that its needs for new protocols are represented in the standards bodies.
sections.plainLanguage: Three ways forward were set out: adopt the ISO protocol as a co-standard immediately, demonstrate it first and then adopt, or keep TCP and decide later. The committee thought all three would meet the department's needs, and chose the first, because it reaches commercial products and outside interoperability soonest, while accepting more risk. Its conclusion was unanimous on the direction, namely adopt the ISO protocols alongside TCP and move towards using only them, and the timing was where the committee split, with most wanting immediate adoption and a few wanting a demonstration first.

items.title: Survivability
items.text: The network must still work, at reduced speed, after many nodes and links have been destroyed.

items.title: Security
items.text: Selected traffic must be protected by encryption, access control, auditing and routing.
